The matrix has \(3\) rows and \(3\) columns, so it is a square matrix of order \(3\). Every element below the main diagonal is zero, since \(a_{21} = a_{31} = a_{32} = 0\), while some element above the diagonal is non-zero.

\(\therefore\) it is an upper triangular matrix.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 & 7 \\ -4 & 0 & -3 \\ -7 & 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 & -7 \\ 4 & 0 & 3 \\ 7 & -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = -A\), and every diagonal entry is \(0\).

\(\therefore\) it is a skew-symmetric matrix.

The matrix has order \(3\times 1\), that is it has only one column.

\(\therefore\) it is a column matrix.

The matrix has order \(1\times 3\), that is it has only one row.

\(\therefore\) it is a row matrix.

It is a square matrix of order \(2\) in which every non-diagonal element is zero, so it is diagonal; moreover both diagonal entries are equal to \(6\), so the matrix is \(6\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(\therefore\) it is a scalar matrix.

It is a square matrix of order \(3\) and every element above the main diagonal is zero, since \(a_{12} = a_{13} = a_{23} = 0\), while some element below the diagonal is non-zero.

\(\therefore\) it is a lower triangular matrix.

It is a square matrix of order \(3\) in which every non-diagonal element is zero, and the diagonal entries \(3\), \(5\), \(\frac{1}{3}\) are not all equal.

\(\therefore\) it is a diagonal matrix.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -15 & 27 \\ -15 & 0 & \sqrt{34} \\ 27 & \sqrt{34} & \frac{5}{3} \end{bmatrix}\). Interchanging rows and columns leaves it unchanged, since \(a_{12} = a_{21} = -15\), \(a_{13} = a_{31} = 27\) and \(a_{23} = a_{32} = \sqrt{34}\), so \(A^{T} = A\).

\(\therefore\) it is a symmetric matrix.

It is a square matrix of order \(3\) with every non-diagonal element zero and every diagonal element equal to \(1\).

\(\therefore\) it is a unit (identity) matrix.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Here \(a_{12} = a_{21} = 0\), \(a_{13} = a_{31} = 1\) and \(a_{23} = a_{32} = 0\), so \(A^{T} = A\). (It is not diagonal, since \(a_{13} = 1 \ne 0\).)

\(\therefore\) it is a symmetric matrix.

Let \(A\) be the given matrix. Its third row is exactly twice the first row minus the second row, that is \(R_3 = 2R_1 - R_2\). Applying \(R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1 + R_2\),

\(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ p & q & r \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0\), since a row is entirely zero.

\(\therefore |A| = 0\), so the matrix is singular.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & 99 & 100 \\ 6 & 99 & 105 \end{bmatrix}\). Here \(R_3 = R_1 + R_2\), since \(5+1 = 6\), \(0+99 = 99\) and \(5+100 = 105\). Applying \(R_3 \to R_3 - R_1 - R_2\) makes the third row entirely zero.

\(\therefore |A| = 0\), so the matrix is singular.

Expanding along the first row,

\(|A| = 3(1\times 5 - 4\times 2) - 5\big((-2)\times 5 - 4\times 3\big) + 7\big((-2)\times 2 - 1\times 3\big)\)

\(= 3(-3) - 5(-22) + 7(-7) = -9 + 110 - 49 = 52\).

\(\therefore |A| = 52 \ne 0\), so the matrix is non-singular.

\(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 7 & 5 \\ -4 & 7 \end{vmatrix} = 7\times 7 - 5\times(-4) = 49 + 20 = 69\).

\(\therefore |A| = 69 \ne 0\), so the matrix is non-singular.

A matrix is singular when its determinant is zero, so

\(\begin{vmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ -2 & k \end{vmatrix} = 0\)

\(7k - 3(-2) = 0\), that is \(7k + 6 = 0\).

\(\therefore k = -\frac{6}{7}\)

For a singular matrix the determinant is zero. Expanding along the first row,

\(4(k\times 1 - 1\times 9) - 3(7\times 1 - 1\times 10) + 1(7\times 9 - k\times 10) = 0\)

\(4(k - 9) - 3(-3) + (63 - 10k) = 0\)

\(4k - 36 + 9 + 63 - 10k = 0\), that is \(-6k + 36 = 0\).

\(\therefore k = 6\)

For a singular matrix the determinant is zero. Expanding along the first row,

\((k-1)\big(1\times 4 - 2\times(-2)\big) - 2(3\times 4 - 2\times 1) + 3\big(3\times(-2) - 1\times 1\big) = 0\)

\((k-1)(8) - 2(10) + 3(-7) = 0\)

\(8k - 8 - 20 - 21 = 0\), that is \(8k = 49\).

\(\therefore k = \frac{49}{8}\)

\(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) (order \(3\times 2\)).

Taking the transpose once more interchanges rows and columns again, so

\((A^{T})^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = A\)

This illustrates the property \((A^{T})^{T} = A\).

\(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -2 & 5 \\ 3 & -4 & 9 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Taking the transpose of this again interchanges rows and columns once more, so

\((A^{T})^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -4 & 1 \\ 5 & 9 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = A\)

This illustrates the property \((A^{T})^{T} = A\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -5 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ -5 & 4 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\). Interchanging its rows and columns,

\(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -5 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ -5 & 4 & 9 \end{bmatrix} = A\).

Since \(A^{T} = A\), the matrix is symmetric.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & 1 \\ -5 & 4 & 6 \\ -1 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Interchanging its rows and columns,

\(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 & -1 \\ 5 & 4 & -6 \\ 1 & 6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Here \(A^{T} \ne A\), since \(a_{12} = 5\) but the corresponding entry of \(A^{T}\) is \(-5\); and \(A^{T} \ne -A\), since the diagonal entry \(2\) of \(A^{T}\) is not \(-2\) (a skew-symmetric matrix must have all diagonal entries zero).

\(\therefore\) the matrix is neither symmetric nor skew-symmetric.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1+2i & i-2 \\ -1-2i & 0 & -7 \\ 2-i & 7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Interchanging its rows and columns,

\(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1-2i & 2-i \\ 1+2i & 0 & 7 \\ i-2 & -7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

Also \(-A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1-2i & 2-i \\ 1+2i & 0 & 7 \\ i-2 & -7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), because \(-(i-2) = 2-i\) and \(-(2-i) = i-2\).

Since \(A^{T} = -A\), the matrix is skew-symmetric.

Here \(i, j = 1, 2, 3\) and \(a_{ij} = i - j\), so every diagonal entry \(a_{ii} = 0\), and

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

Then \(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = -A\); this also follows from \(a_{ji} = j - i = -(i-j) = -a_{ij}\).

\(\therefore A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and A is a skew-symmetric matrix.
